newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FEATURE - Portugal's Communists still proud to be red.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Portugal's Communists still proud to be red.

text.p: Portugal's unrepentant Communist Party may be one of the few orthodox Marxist parties left in western Europe, but it is far from feeling an endangered species.

The party, which won just under 10 percent of the vote in elections a year ago -- enough for 15 seats in the 230-seat parliament -- is gearing itself up to spearhead battles for higher wages and to mobilise opinion against a pet hate, the Maastricht Treaty which binds Portugal to the European Union.
"Our influence within society is greater than our political weight," party secretary-general Carlos Carvalhas told Reuters in an interview.

Party support has fallen from a peak of 19 percent in elections in 1979, the second following Portugal's return to democracy in an armed forces' revolt in 1974. But besides its parliamentary presence, it remains a signficant force within the trades unions.

Carvalhas, who took over from the fiercely hardline Alvaro Cunhal four years ago, was confident that the economic line being followed by Portugal's Socialist government could only boost support for what he said were genuine left-wing solutions.

"The (Socialist) policy is not left-wing. It is the same policy that was defeated in the ballot," he said, referring to the Socialists' electoral victory in October 1995 that ended a decade of conservative rule by the Social Democrats.
"We think that these policies are going to create a lot of frustration very quickly, they are going to create discontent in important sectors of the population," he said.
Politically, the government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres amounted to an "alternation but not an alternative" to the previous administration, Carvalhas said.

The Communist-led Common Front union alliance, the country's largest, is preparing to take on the government over its plans to hold public sector wage rises to the expected 2.5 percent inflation rate seen for next year.
The government says that any more would jeopardise its hopes of passing a series of tough economic tests being set for entry to the European Union's single currency.
But for 54-year-old Carvalhas higher wages would not only be socially just, they would also give a shot in the arm to Portugal's still anaemic economy.
The mild-mannered economist lacks the charisma and aura of heroism that surrounds the still-active Cunhal, but he is no more ready than his legendary predecessor to turn his back on his party's past.

His election in 1992 did not herald a party renewal and the sort of reassessment, for example, that eventually led the Italian Communist Party, once the biggest in the West, to shed its name and its ideology.
Almost 40 years to the day since Moscow's troops crushed the Hungarian uprising, one of the blackest moments of the Soviet era, Portugal's communists remain proud of their name and their roots.

The failure of the Eastern European model is attributed by the party, which publicly rejected the perestroika reforms of former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, to communist leaders having strayed from true Marxist ideas and ideals.
"We are very honoured to be communists. There is nothing in our past which dishonours us. On the contrary, we are very proud," Carvalhas said.
It is in fact the past which explains much of the lingering support in Portugal for the Communist Party.

Cunhal was one of the symbols of resistance to the right-wing dictatorship of Antonio Salazar who died in 1970, four years before the final collapse of his system of government amidst the chaos of the colonial wars.

The communists came close to winning power with the backing of radical military officers in the heady days that followed the "carnation' revolution, so called because soldiers stuck flowers in their gun barrels during the largely peaceful takeover.

But the importance of the past is also reflected in the age of the party membership. According to a recent report in the Expresso newspaper, less than 10 percent of the party membership is under 30 and too young to remember the years of dictatorship.

For Carvalhas, communism remains a noble notion of a more just and caring society. Capitalism "does not resolve the problems." But the road to communism lay through ever-greater democracy -- economic, cultural and social.
In the meantime, tax rises for the better off to redistribute the country's wealth offered a solution to pressing problems of how to finance the pension and creaking social welfare systems.
The change of leadership may have left the ideology and the political message intact, but the style has evolved.

The beady-eyed Cunhal was rarely seen with a tie. But for campaign posters during the 1995 election, Carvalhas posed neatly attired in a dark suit and tie that would have not have been out of place in a company boardroom.
Carvalhas shrugs off any suggestion of massaging the image. He says he just feels more comfortable with a tie.
